epilobe.resume: Tall pink spikes in forest clearings, felled areas and mountain glades.
identification: Upright stems up to 1.5 m
Narrow lance-shaped leaves, veins that join in loops near the edge
Clusters of bright pink flowers in summer
usages: Young shoots cooked like asparagus.
Dried leaves as a tea.

chamois.resume: Agile on steep slopes, it whistles when it's worried.
identification: Brown coat in summer, almost black in winter
White and black face mask
Small black horns curved into a hook
usages: Watch from a distance, without making it flee down the slopes, especially in winter when every effort exhausts it.

marmotte.resume: Whistles to warn the others. Hibernates from October to April.
identification: Large grey-brown rodent sitting near its burrow
Sharp warning whistle
usages: Don't feed them: human food makes them ill.

patou.resume: Large white dogs guarding flocks in mountain pastures. They protect the sheep, not the hikers.
identification: Large white or cream dog, often alone in the middle of or near a flock
Barks and comes towards walkers
usages: Go well around the flock. Get off your bike and walk.
Stop calmly if it approaches, don't shout, don't threaten it with a stick, don't stare at it.
Let it identify you, then move on slowly without turning your back abruptly.
Keep your own dog on a lead, close to you.

salicorne.resume: A crunchy, naturally salty plant of salt marshes.
identification: Small fleshy plant with no visible leaves, stems jointed in segments
Grows in the mud of salt marshes, flooded at high tide
usages: Raw or blanched, without adding salt.
Picking is often regulated or banned in nature reserves: check first.

argousier.resume: A spiny dune shrub with orange berries very rich in vitamin C.
identification: Very spiny shrub, narrow silvery leaves
Bright orange berries packed along the twigs
usages: Very sour berries: as juice or cooked.
Cutting a twig damages the shrub: pick by hand, with gloves.

vive.resume: A small fish buried in the sand of beaches at low tide. Its dorsal spines inject a very painful venom.
identification: Small yellow-brown fish 10 to 15 cm, buried in the sand
Black, spiny dorsal fin
usages: Wear water shoes on sand at low tide.
If stung: put the foot in the hottest water you can bear (without scalding) for 30 minutes, because heat destroys the venom. See a doctor if you feel faint or the swelling is large.

meduse.resume: Some cause sharp stings, even when washed up on the beach.
identification: Gelatinous umbrella-shaped body, long tentacles
Never touch a stranded jellyfish
usages: Get out of the water, rinse with seawater (not fresh water, which bursts the stinging cells).
Remove the tentacles with a card or tweezers, without rubbing.
Call 112 if breathing becomes difficult or you feel faint.

massette.saison: Shoots Apr.–Jun., rhizomes all year round
massette.resume: The “cigar reed” of ponds and ditches. Almost the whole plant is edible, but it also concentrates water pollutants.
identification: Long, thick, spongy strap-like leaves, sheathed inside each other at the base
Brown sausage-shaped spike at the top of a long stem in summer
Grows with its feet in the water, in large colonies

sosies.diff: Flat leaves arranged in a fan, stiffer, no spongy sheath; large yellow flowers in spring. Poisonous.

usages: Young spring shoots: the white heart, raw or cooked.
Rhizomes: peeled and cooked, rich in starch.
Only in clean water, away from roads, fields and outflows.

iris.resume: Grows in the same places as the bulrush, and gets confused with it when not in flower.
identification: Flat, stiff leaves in a fan
Large yellow flowers in May–June
Thick rhizome
usages: Eat nothing. The sap can irritate the skin.

truite.resume: The wild trout of cool streams and rivers like the Ourthe. Excellent cooked, but tightly controlled by fishing rules.
identification: Streamlined body, brown-green back
Black spots and red spots ringed with pale on the flanks
Small adipose fin (no rays) between the dorsal fin and the tail
Lives in clear, cool, well-oxygenated water

sosies.diff: More forked tail, a row of dark marks on the flanks (parr marks), no ringed red spots. Protected: release it.
Pinkish-purple band along the flank, small black spots right onto the tail. A stocked farmed fish, edible.

usages: Barbless hooks are required in many sectors of Wallonia: check before fishing.
Cook right through: the flesh turns opaque and flakes.
A trout keeps a few hours in the cool: gutted, in the shade, wrapped in damp grass.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

perche.resume: One of the best freshwater fish, common in still water and slow rivers. Beware the spines of the dorsal fin.
identification: Dark vertical stripes on a greenish body
Large spiny dorsal fin with a black spot at the back
Orange-red belly fins

sosies.diff: Smaller, no clear stripes, covered in small dots. Also edible.

usages: Grab the perch by folding the dorsal fin back with your hand, so you don't get pricked.
May carry a parasitic worm (fish tapeworm): never raw, always well cooked.
Easy to scale right after catching.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

brochet.resume: The big predator of still waters. Its flesh is good, but it has sharp teeth and many Y-shaped bones.
identification: Very elongated body, duck-bill head
Green flanks marbled with pale spots
Dorsal and anal fins set right at the back
Mouth full of pointed teeth

sosies.diff: Two dorsal fins, one spiny, large glassy eyes, striped grey flanks.

usages: Never put your fingers in its mouth: use pliers or a stick to unhook it.
May carry the fish tapeworm: always well cooked, never as tartare or raw-marinated.
Big fish build up more pollutants: prefer medium-sized ones.
In Wallonia, keeping pike is restricted in some areas: check the rules.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

sandre.resume: A predator of slow rivers, canals and murky lakes. Firm white flesh, highly prized.
identification: Elongated grey-green body with blurred dark bands
Two dorsal fins, the first spiny
Large glassy eyes and a few big teeth (fangs)

sosies.diff: Stockier, clear stripes, orange belly fins.

usages: Watch out for the dorsal spines and the fangs.
Cook well, like all freshwater fish.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

gardon.resume: The most common “white fish”. Easy to catch, edible, but full of small bones.
identification: Small silvery fish with a blue-green back
Eye with a red iris
Reddish belly and anal fins

sosies.diff: Brighter red fins, upturned mouth. Also edible.

usages: The small bones soften when deep-fried very hot or cooked for a long time.
Like all white fish: never raw, some carry liver parasites.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

chevesne.resume: A large, stocky white fish, very common in the Ourthe and Ardennes rivers. Not much prized because of its bones.
identification: Thick body, large broad head
Large black-edged scales, in a net pattern
Convex, reddish-orange anal fin

sosies.diff: Slimmer, small head, concave (hollowed) anal fin.

usages: Fillet it and score the fillets finely every 3 mm before cooking: the bones become unnoticeable.
Cook well.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

carpe.resume: A large fish of still, muddy waters. Old specimens root in the mud and build up pollutants.
identification: Large golden to bronze body
Four barbels around the mouth
Large scales (or few scales in mirror carp)

sosies.diff: Smaller, no barbels.

usages: Prefer small carp: large ones (over 5 kg) build up more pollutants.
Remove the skin, the belly fat and the brown line along the flank, where the muddy taste and pollutants concentrate.
Night fishing for carp needs a specific permit in Wallonia.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

barbeau.resume: A bottom fish of flowing rivers, like the Ourthe. Its flesh is edible, but its roe is poisonous.
identification: Elongated body, flat belly
Mouth under the head with four barbels
Brown-green back, reddish fins

sosies.diff: Very small (under 15 cm), only two barbels, dark spots on the flanks.

usages: NEVER eat barbel roe, especially in spring: it causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
Gut it well and remove the whole roe sac.
Lots of bones: best as scored fillets or in soup.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

silure.resume: The giant of our rivers, more and more common in the Meuse and its tributaries. Young, it's good; old, it concentrates pollutants.
identification: Very long scaleless, slimy body
Wide mouth with six barbels, two of them very long
Tiny fin on the back, very long anal fin

sosies.diff: Much smaller (under 35 cm), eight barbels, hard spines on the fins.

usages: Prefer fish under 1 m.
Remove the skin and fat.
Careful: a big catfish is very powerful, never wrap the line around your hand.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

poissonchat.resume: A small introduced North American fish, invasive in still waters. Edible, but its spines sting badly.
identification: Scaleless body, brown-black, broad head
Eight barbels
A hard spine at the front of the dorsal fin and of each pectoral fin

sosies.diff: Six barbels, no spine on the back, very long anal fin.

usages: Grab it behind the pectoral spines, or with a thick cloth.
A sting is very painful and gets infected easily: see the fiche on spine and tooth wounds.
Invasive species: never release it alive elsewhere or carry it alive.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

anguille.resume: A critically endangered species. In Wallonia, every eel caught must be put back. It is also one of the fish most loaded with pollutants (PCBs, dioxins).
identification: Snake-like body, no belly fins
Dorsal, tail and anal fins fused into a single fringe
Slimy skin, small head with small eyes

sosies.diff: No jaw but a sucker mouth, seven round holes behind the eye. Protected.

usages: Unhook it in the water and release it straight away.
Its raw blood irritates eyes and wounds: rinse your hands after touching it.
Even elsewhere, don't eat it: eels in our rivers often exceed pollutant limits.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

saumon.resume: It vanished from the Meuse in the 20th century and is being reintroduced. Every fish counts: it must be released at once.
identification: Young (parr): a row of dark marks on the flanks, clearly forked tail
Adult: silvery body, small black cross-shaped spots above the lateral line
Small adipose fin on the back

sosies.diff: Red spots ringed with pale, less forked tail.

usages: Release it by holding it in the water, facing the current, until it swims off on its own.
Reporting a catch to the Maison wallonne de la Pêche helps monitor the reintroduction.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

ombre.resume: The “fish with the big sail”, a sign of very pure water. Its populations are fragile: release it.
identification: Very large, colourful sail-shaped dorsal fin
Silvery-grey body with a few black spots at the front
Small adipose fin

sosies.diff: Small dorsal fin, red spots.

usages: Grayling rules are very strict and change from one sector to another: if in doubt, release it.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

chabot.resume: A small big-headed bottom fish, hidden under the stones of clean streams. Protected in Europe.
identification: Under 15 cm, very large flattened head
Large fan-shaped pectoral fins
Marbled brown scaleless body, lives under pebbles

sosies.diff: Long, slim body, six barbels, small head.

usages: Don't turn over stream stones to look for it: they shelter it and many larvae.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

ecrevisse_rouge.resume: The native crayfish, now very rare because of diseases brought by American crayfish. Strictly protected.
identification: Large dark brown crayfish
Bright red underside to the claws
Broad, grainy claws

sosies.diff: White or turquoise patch at the claw joint, smooth claws. Invasive.

usages: Release it on the spot immediately.
After handling American crayfish, dry boots and gear before going into another stream: you could carry crayfish plague.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

ecrevisse_signal.resume: An introduced, invasive American crayfish, carrying a disease deadly to the native crayfish. Edible and excellent cooked.
identification: Large bluish-brown crayfish
White or turquoise patch on the claw joint
Red underside to the claws

sosies.diff: No pale patch on the claws, grainy claws. Protected: release it.
Smaller, rusty patches on the sides of the abdomen, orange-tipped claws.

usages: Always well cooked (5 to 10 minutes in boiling water): it can carry parasites.
Remove the black gut from the tail before eating.
Carrying it alive is banned: an invasive species at EU level.
Catching crayfish is regulated: check the local rules.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

grandevive.resume: The bigger cousin of the lesser weever, sometimes caught on a line from beaches or boats. Its spines stay venomous even after the fish is dead.
identification: Up to 40 cm, elongated yellow-brown body
Fine dark oblique stripes on the flanks
Short, black, spiny first dorsal fin

sosies.diff: Smaller and stockier, lives buried near the shore.

usages: The spines stay dangerous on a dead fish or on the fish counter: handle with a thick cloth.
Edible once the spines have been removed by someone experienced.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

rascasse.resume: A Mediterranean rock fish, a master of camouflage. Very good to eat (bouillabaisse), but its spines are venomous.
identification: Stocky body, mottled red-brown, covered in skin flaps
Large spiny head, big eyes
Dorsal fin bristling with spines

sosies.diff: Long, smooth body, lives on sand.

usages: Never grab with bare hands: thick gloves or a cloth.
Sting: very hot water, as for the weever.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.

vairon.resume: A tiny fish of clear streams, in shoals. A sign of good water quality, and food for trout.
identification: Under 10 cm, in tight shoals
Flanks mottled with dark patches, belly sometimes red in spring
Very small scales

sosies.diff: Silvery, red eye, large scales.

usages: Don't use it as live bait if the species isn't on the list of allowed baitfish: check the rules.
Too small to be worth eating, except in real distress, fried whole and well cooked.

notes.BE: In Wallonia, a fishing permit is required on public rivers, canals and lakes. Open seasons, minimum sizes and quotas depend on the species: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche.
